title: Menelaus as a mother cow over her calf
greek: περὶ πόρτακι μήτηρ πρωτοτόκος κινυρή (peri portaki mētēr prōtotokos kinurē)
short: Menelaus straddles Patroclus' body like a cow lowing over her first calf: a tender, domestic image for a warrior defending a corpse.
body: The book opens with a posture that dominates it: a fighter 'bestriding' (amphibainein) a fallen comrade to keep the enemy off the body. Elsewhere this stance is compared to a lion (Aeneas over Pandarus, 5.299), but here the poet chooses a young cow who has just calved for the first time and stands over her calf, lowing plaintively. Leaf observes that the point lies only in the mother's anxious care for her young; we should not imagine a beast of prey attacking her. The image fits the Menelaus of Book 17, a warrior of loyalty rather than overwhelming strength, who later praises Patroclus for his gentleness (17.670-2). It also starts a chain of parental images that runs through the fight for the body: Ajax as a lion protecting its cubs (17.133-6), and Achilles as a lion robbed of its cubs (18.318-22). The struggle over Patroclus is presented as a struggle of kin and of love, not merely of spoil.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, 2nd ed., vol. 2 (Macmillan, 1902), note on 17.4

title: The uprooted olive sapling
greek: ἔρνος ... ἐριθηλὲς ἐλαίης (ernos ... erithēles elaiēs)
short: Euphorbus falls like a carefully tended olive shoot torn up by a sudden storm: the Iliad's image for a young life cut off.
body: A man raises an olive shoot in a lonely, well-watered spot; it quivers in every wind and bursts into white blossom, until a sudden gale tears it from its trench and lays it on the ground. The simile stresses nurture: someone 'reared' (trephei) the tree, just as Euphorbus has just spoken of the grief of his parents Panthous and Phrontis. The ernos, 'young shoot', becomes a key word for doomed youth: Thetis twice says of Achilles that 'he shot up like a sapling' (ernei isos, 18.56-7, 18.437-8), and Leaf, commenting on that line, links it with this passage and with Odysseus' comparison of Nausicaa to a young palm-shoot at Delos (Od. 6.162). Compare also the poplar simile for the young Simoeisius (4.482-7). Such tree similes make a warrior's death a loss to a household and a landscape, not only to an army.

title: Euphorbus, son of Panthous
greek: Πάνθου υἱὸν ἐϋμμελίην Εὔφορβον (Panthou huion eummeliēn Euphorbon)
short: The young Trojan who first wounded Patroclus is killed by Menelaus; later Greeks saw his shield at Argos and Pythagoras claimed to have been him.
body: Euphorbus, son of the Trojan elder Panthous and brother of Polydamas, had struck Patroclus first from behind (16.806-15) before Hector delivered the death-blow. Here he claims the spoils and is killed by Menelaus, and the poet gives him one of the most delicate death-pieces in the poem: his blood soaks hair 'like the hair of the Graces', its locks pinched with gold and silver. Leaf notes that small gold spirals have been found lying beside the head in graves, with parallels from Etruria, Greece and Hissarlik (Troy), so the detail reflects real Bronze Age fashion. Euphorbus had an afterlife outside Homer. Pausanias (2.17.3) saw in the Argive Heraeum a votive shield said to be the one Menelaus took from him. Pythagoras claimed that his own soul had once lived in Euphorbus, the man 'wounded by Menelaus' (Diogenes Laertius 8.4-5, citing Heraclides of Pontus); Ovid retells the story in Metamorphoses 15.160-4.

title: Apollo disguised as Mentes of the Cicones
greek: Κικόνων ἡγήτορι Μέντῃ (Kikonōn hēgētori Mentēi)
short: Apollo rouses Hector in the shape of Mentes, a Thracian ally; Book 17 is full of gods who act in mortal disguise.
body: The Cicones were a Thracian people allied to Troy; in the Trojan Catalogue they are led by Euphemus (2.846), and Leaf notes the discrepancy (Mentes is not heard of again, and some scholia read the name as Peiros). In the Odyssey they are the first people Odysseus raids after leaving Troy, at Ismarus (Od. 9.39-61). The name Mentes appears again in Od. 1.105, where Athena disguises herself as 'Mentes, leader of the Taphians'. The scene is typical of this book, in which gods repeatedly intervene in borrowed shapes: Apollo as Periphas the herald to Aeneas (17.322-6), Athena as old Phoenix to Menelaus (17.555), Apollo as Phaenops to Hector (17.582-3). Sometimes the mortal recognises the god (Aeneas does, 17.333-4); sometimes he does not. Disguise lets the gods steer the battle while human choice and responsibility remain visible.

title: Menelaus' deliberation: 'Why does my heart debate this?'
greek: ἀλλὰ τί ἤ μοι ταῦτα φίλος διελέξατο θυμός; (alla ti ē moi tauta philos dielexato thumos)
short: One of four Iliadic monologues in which a lone hero weighs flight against shame, using the same turning line; Menelaus alone decides to withdraw.
body: Four times in the Iliad a warrior left alone against superior numbers speaks to his own 'great-hearted spirit' (thumos): Odysseus (11.404-10), Menelaus here, Agenor (21.553-70) and Hector before Achilles (22.99-130). Each weighs the shame of retreat against the danger of staying and then breaks off with the same line, 'But why does my heart debate these things with me?' Bernard Fenik's study of these four speeches shows how a fixed pattern is varied to fit each character. Menelaus is the only one who resolves to give ground, and he justifies it in religious terms: to fight a man 'whom a god honours' brings disaster, so no Achaean will blame him. His fear of blame (nemesis) from his own side shows the pressure of aidos, shame before one's peers, on Homeric decisions. Compare Hector, whose monologue ends in the opposite decision and in his death.

title: The threat to Patroclus' corpse
greek: ἀπ᾽ ὤμοιιν κεφαλὴν τάμοι ὀξέϊ χαλκῷ (ap' ōmoiin kephalēn tamoi oxei chalkōi)
short: Hector means to behead Patroclus and throw the body to the dogs of Troy: the Iliad's recurring horror of a corpse left unburied and mutilated.
body: From its first lines (1.4-5) the Iliad dwells on bodies made 'a prey for dogs and birds'. Hector's intention to cut off Patroclus' head and give the body to the dogs is the most explicit statement of that threat so far; Iris repeats it in 18.175-7, adding that he wants to fix the head on 'the stakes of the wall', which Leaf takes to be a palisade on top of the Trojan wall (cf. Od. 7.45). Leaf's Companion remarks that mutilation mattered more to the Greeks than to us, since a maimed body was thought to leave the spirit maimed too. The threat is reversed in the poem's design: Achilles will drag Hector's corpse and plan to feed it to dogs (22.335-54, 23.21), until the gods preserve the body and Priam ransoms it (Book 24). Leaf also notes that here Patroclus is still imagined as wearing armour, which sits awkwardly with Apollo's stripping of it in 16.793-804.

anchor: as a lion over his whelps
title: Ajax as a lion over its cubs
greek: ὥς τίς τε λέων περὶ οἷσι τέκεσσιν ... πᾶν δέ τ᾽ ἐπισκύνιον κάτω ἕλκεται (hōs tis te leōn peri hoisi tekessin ... pan de t' episkunion katō helketai)
short: Ajax covers Patroclus with his tower-shield like a lion guarding its cubs from hunters, drawing its brow down over its eyes.
body: Ajax arrives with his famous shield 'like a city wall' and stands over the body as a lion stands over its young when huntsmen meet it in the forest. The odd detail that the lion 'draws down all its brows to cover its eyes' had an ancient explanation, quoted by Leaf from the scholia: the lioness defending her cubs lowers her brow so as not to see the spears and lose her nerve. Leaf's note on 17.134-6 also records that Zenodotus and the Chian edition omitted these lines because it is the lioness, not the lion, who leads the cubs. The simile turns Ajax's defence into a parent's protection of a child and prepares a deliberate contrast in the next book, where the grieving Achilles is a lion whose cubs a hunter has already taken (18.318-22).

title: Glaucus' rebuke: Sarpedon as guest-friend and comrade
greek: Σαρπηδόν᾽ ἅμα ξεῖνον καὶ ἑταῖρον (Sarpēdon' hama xeinon kai hetairon)
short: The Lycian Glaucus accuses Hector of abandoning Sarpedon, his guest-friend and comrade, and threatens to take the Lycians home.
body: Glaucus speaks for the allies, whose loyalty rests on reciprocity. Sarpedon was Hector's xeinos (guest-friend, bound by the obligations of xenia) and hetairos (comrade), and had often 'proved a boon' to Troy; Hector's failure to protect his body breaks that bond, so 'there were to be no thanks' for the Lycians' toil. Sarpedon himself had explained, in his famous speech to Glaucus (12.310-28), that kings fight in front because of the honours their people give them; Glaucus now applies the same logic of exchange to the alliance. His proposal, to trade Patroclus' body for Sarpedon's armour and corpse, rests on a misunderstanding: Leaf points out that Glaucus evidently does not know that Apollo, on Zeus' orders, carried Sarpedon's body away to Lycia (16.667-83). Hector's angry reply, that Zeus' will is stronger than any man's courage, introduces the theme of divine favour that runs through the book.

title: Hector puts on the armour of Achilles
greek: ἀλλ᾽ οὐχ υἱὸς ἐν ἔντεσι πατρὸς ἐγήρα (all' ouch huios en entesi patros egēra)
short: Hector dons the immortal armour the gods gave Peleus; the narrator and Zeus himself foresee that neither Achilles nor Hector will live long in it.
body: The armour was a wedding gift of the gods to Peleus (18.84-5), passed to Achilles, lent to Patroclus and now stripped by Hector. The narrator adds a quiet prophecy: the son did not grow old in his father's armour. Zeus then pities Hector: 'death is not in your thoughts, yet it is near'; he will grant him great might now, 'in recompense' (apoina) because he will never come home for Andromache to take the armour from him. Zeus also says Hector took the arms 'not in seemly wise' (ou kata kosmon). The exchange of armour binds the three deaths together: Hector will die in Achilles' old armour, pierced where it leaves the throat exposed (22.321-7). Some analytic critics have treated the passage as a later insertion; most modern readers see the armour as part of the poem's design.

title: Hector and the economics of the Trojan alliance
greek: μυρία φῦλα περικτιόνων ἐπικούρων ... δώροισι κατατρύχω καὶ ἐδωδῇ λαούς (muria phula periktionōn epikourōn ... dōroisi katatruchō kai edōdēi laous)
short: Hector reminds the allies that he drains his own people to pay them in gifts and food, and promises half the spoils to whoever wins Patroclus' body.
body: Hector's speech shows how the Trojan war effort is paid for. He has not gathered the allies for their numbers, he says, but to protect Trojan wives and children, and to support them he 'wears out' his own people with gifts and provisions. Leaf's Companion links this with Hector's complaint in 18.288-92 that Troy's famous treasures have been sold off to Phrygia and Maeonia: a long siege is ruinous for the besieged. The reward he offers is shaped by the same economy of honour: half the spoils for whoever drags Patroclus into Troy, and 'his glory shall be even as mine own'. The speech closes with a striking phrase, 'this is the dalliance of war' (oaristus, literally the intimate talk of lovers): grim irony for the meeting of fighters who must kill or die. Compare Hector's later use of the same idea before Achilles (22.126-8).

title: Drinking 'at the common cost'
greek: δήμια πίνουσιν (dēmia pinousin)
short: Menelaus appeals to the chiefs who drink at the public expense at the table of the sons of Atreus: honour brings obligations in battle.
body: The leading chiefs of the Achaeans dine and drink at the king's table, and the cost is borne by the community (dēmia, 'at the public cost'). Leaf explains the system: the king receives gifts from his people and in return offers hospitality to the chiefs (compare 2.404, 4.257-64, where Agamemnon praises Idomeneus' privileged cup, and 9.70-3, Nestor's reminder that Agamemnon's huts are full of wine). Such privileges are a visible form of timē (honour), and Menelaus' appeal draws the consequence: those who enjoy 'honour and glory from Zeus' must now earn it by defending Patroclus. Sarpedon makes the same argument to Glaucus about Lycian kingship (12.310-21). Leaf notes small difficulties in the passage, for example that Menelaus is nowhere else a public host alongside his brother, but does not think the lines should be removed.

title: Zeus' darkness over the fight for the body
greek: Κρονίων ἠέρα πολλὴν χεῦ᾽ (Kroniōn ēera pollēn cheu')
short: Zeus wraps the fighters around Patroclus in thick mist, while the rest of the battle goes on in clear sunshine.
body: Zeus spreads a thick mist (aēr) over the helmets of the Achaeans around the body, because he had not hated Patroclus while he lived and does not want him to become sport for Trojan dogs. Later the poet contrasts the darkness over the chiefs at the centre with the bright sun, cloudless sky and leisurely fighting elsewhere (17.366-77). Leaf found the supernatural darkness hard to accept: in his view Zeus' help is 'singularly ill-judged', since the Achaeans are the first to pray for its removal (17.645-7), and he suspected 268-73 of being a later addition; he suggested the darkness of Ajax's prayer might simply be the dust of battle. Other readers take the mist as deliberate symbolism, isolating the chosen few who fight in confusion around the corpse. The motif culminates in Ajax's prayer for light.

title: Repaying parents for one's rearing (threptra)
greek: οὐδὲ τοκεῦσι θρέπτρα φίλοις ἀπέδωκε (oude tokeusi threptra philois apedōke)
short: Killed young, Hippothous cannot repay his parents for raising him, the care children owed parents in old age.
body: Greek society expected children to repay the 'cost of rearing' (threptra) by supporting their parents in old age. A warrior who dies young leaves that debt unpaid, and the Iliad uses the same two lines for the young Simoeisius (4.477-9); Leaf notes the repetition. Hesiod (Works and Days 185-8) makes the failure to repay aged parents a sign of the degenerate Iron Age. The victim here, Hippothous, son of 'Pelasgian Lethus', comes 'from deep-soiled Larissa'. Leaf's Companion notes that there were many towns called Larisa and that ancient tradition took the word as Pelasgian for 'citadel', which suits a Pelasgian hero; the Pelasgians' Larisa is also named in the Trojan Catalogue (2.840-3). The short obituary, with home, parents and unpaid debt, is a typical Iliadic way of giving a minor victim a life.

title: 'Beyond the allotment of Zeus' (hyper Dios aisan)
greek: ὑπὲρ Διὸς αἶσαν (huper Dios aisan)
short: The Achaeans would have won glory even beyond Zeus' allotted portion, had Apollo not intervened: one of Homer's 'if not' moments.
body: Homer often says that something would have happened 'beyond fate' (huper moron, 2.155, 16.780, 20.30) or here 'beyond the portion (aisa) of Zeus', had a god not intervened. Leaf refers the reader to his notes on 2.155 and 16.780 for the expression. Such 'if not' situations show that the story could in principle go another way, and they mark the moment when divine action keeps it on its known course. Aisa, 'share, portion', is close in meaning to moira; the phrase 'aisa of Zeus' shows how fate and the will of Zeus are bound together without being simply identical. Apollo's speech to Aeneas makes the same point from the other side: men have held their cities even against Zeus by courage (17.327-31, a line restored by Brocks' conjecture, which Leaf's Companion calls brilliant), but now Zeus favours Troy and they hold back.

anchor: the hide of a great bull
title: The tug-of-war: stretching the oiled bull's hide
greek: ταύροιο βοὸς μεγάλοιο βοείην λαοῖσιν δώῃ τανύειν (tauroio boos megaloio boeiēn laoisin dōēi tanuein)
short: Both armies haul at Patroclus' corpse like workmen stretching a greased hide in a circle; then Zeus himself 'stretches' the toil of battle taut.
body: A man gives his people a bull's hide soaked in fat; they stand in a circle and pull until the moisture goes out, the fat soaks in and the hide is stretched to the full. Leaf's Companion explains the craft: leather was cured by stretching and rubbing in oil, a process still used in his day. The simile catches the grotesque reality of the fight, a body pulled to and fro 'in scant space'. Its key verb, tanuein ('to stretch'), is picked up at once in a metaphor: 'such evil toil of men and horses did Zeus on that day strain taut (etanusse) over Patroclus' (17.400-1; again 17.543). Elsewhere Zeus and Poseidon are said to pull the 'rope of strife' tight over both armies (13.358-60). Battle is imagined as a cord drawn tight by the gods, with men caught in the middle.

title: What Achilles knew: Thetis' secret prophecies
greek: πολλάκι γὰρ τό γε μητρὸς ἐπεύθετο νόσφιν ἀκούων (pollaki gar to ge mētros epeutheto nosphin akouōn)
short: Achilles does not yet know Patroclus is dead; Thetis often told him Zeus' plans in private, but not this.
body: The narrator explains why Achilles still expects Patroclus back: he knew from his mother that Patroclus would not sack Troy, but she did not tell him of this disaster. The passage raises a famous problem. At the opening of Book 18 Achilles recalls that Thetis had once told him 'the best of the Myrmidons' would die at Trojan hands while he still lived (18.9-11). Leaf's Companion sees a contradiction and suggests the two passages are of independent origin, though he admits it concerns a minor point; others reconcile them by assuming the earlier prophecy was too vague for Achilles to apply until he sees the rout. Thetis' privileged knowledge of fate recurs throughout the poem (1.414-18; 9.410-16; 18.95-6). The gap between what Achilles knows and what the audience knows gives Antilochus' message its full force.

title: 'The iron din' and 'the brazen heaven'
greek: σιδήρειος δ᾽ ὀρυμαγδὸς χάλκεον οὐρανὸν ἷκε (sidēreios d' orumagdos chalkeon ouranon hike)
short: The noise of battle is 'iron', unyielding and unwearying, and rises to a sky imagined as a solid dome of bronze.
body: Homer's heroes fight with bronze weapons, but iron, the harder everyday metal of the poet's own age, supplies metaphors of hardness and endurance: an 'iron heart' (24.205, 24.521), the 'iron might' of fire (23.177). Leaf glosses 'iron' here as 'indomitable, unwearying'. 'Brazen' (chalkeos) is a standing epithet of the sky, pictured as a solid dome of bronze (compare 5.504 and the 'much-bronze' heaven of Od. 3.2). The line marks a transition: the din of men rises through the air to heaven, and the scene shifts at once to the immortal horses of Achilles weeping apart from the battle and to Zeus watching them.

title: The immortal horses weep for Patroclus
greek: ὥς τε στήλη μένει ἔμπεδον, ἥ τ᾽ ἐπὶ τύμβῳ ... (hōs te stēlē menei empedon, hē t' epi tumbōi)
short: Achilles' immortal horses stand motionless and weep for their charioteer, heads bowed to the ground like a gravestone on a tomb.
body: Xanthus and Balius, sired by the West Wind (16.149-51) and given by the gods to Peleus (16.381, 16.867; Apollodorus 3.13.5 names Poseidon as the giver), refuse to move either back to the ships or into battle. They stand 'as a pillar abideth firm that standeth on the tomb of a dead man or woman', heads bowed to the earth (Leaf calls the verb a strong, picturesque word for heads touching the ground), hot tears falling and manes trailing in the dust. The simile of the grave stēlē turns the horses into a funeral monument for Patroclus before any funeral has been held. Leaf's Companion, otherwise severe on Book 17, calls the mourning of the horses and the speech of Zeus that follows 'one gem of lovely poetry'. One of these horses will later speak to Achilles and foretell his death (19.404-17).

title: Zeus: nothing is more wretched than man
greek: οὐ μὲν γάρ τί πού ἐστιν ὀϊζυρώτερον ἀνδρὸς πάντων (ou men gar ti pou estin oizurōteron andros pantōn)
short: Pitying the horses, Zeus regrets giving immortal creatures to a mortal, and states the poem's bleakest truth about human life.
body: Zeus asks why the gods gave ageless, deathless horses to Peleus, 'a mortal': was it so that they too should share the sorrows of wretched men? He then speaks a general truth: of all things that breathe and move on earth, nothing is more miserable than man. Leaf compares Odysseus' words to Amphinomus, 'nothing feebler does earth nurture than man' (Od. 18.130-1), and notes that the comparative oizurōteron is formed irregularly for metrical reasons. The speech recalls Thetis' own fate, a goddess unwillingly married to a mortal (18.432-4), and anticipates Achilles' words to Priam about the jars of Zeus from which men receive mixed or wholly evil lots (24.525-33). Zeus then gives the horses strength to carry Automedon away and promises glory to the Trojans only until sunset, a limit fulfilled when Hera sends the sun down early (18.239-42).

anchor: on the knees of the gods
title: 'On the knees of the gods'
greek: θεῶν ἐν γούνασι κεῖται (theōn en gounasi keitai)
short: A proverbial phrase meaning that the outcome rests with the gods; it may come from laying offerings on the knees of seated statues.
body: Automedon throws his spear and says the result 'lies on the knees of the gods'; the same phrase recurs at 20.435 and Od. 1.267. Its origin is obscure. Leaf's preferred explanation connects it with the custom seen in 6.90-2 and 6.302-3, where the Trojan women lay a robe on the knees of Athena's seated statue: a gift placed there was surrendered to divine control, so 'on the knees of the gods' means 'no longer in human hands'. A biblical parallel often cited is Proverbs 16:33 ('The lot is cast into the lap; but the whole disposing thereof is of the Lord'). Other explanations link the knees with spinning thread on the lap, as the Fates spin a man's lot (compare 20.127-8, 24.209-10), but none is certain. The formula expresses the typical Homeric balance between human effort ('I too will cast') and divine decision.

title: The 'lurid rainbow' (porphyreē iris)
greek: πορφυρέην ἶριν (porphureēn irin)
short: For Homer the rainbow is an omen of war or storm, not of hope; Athena descends wrapped in a cloud as dark and portentous as a rainbow.
body: Zeus stretches a rainbow from heaven as a portent (teras) of war or of storm, and Athena, wrapped in a 'lurid' (porphureē) cloud, enters the Achaean ranks like it. Leaf stresses that to the Greeks the rainbow carried no associations of hope or comfort; it belonged to the storm-cloud and brought thoughts of gloom and disaster (compare the rainbow-like serpents on Agamemnon's breastplate, 'a portent for mortal men', 11.27-8). The adjective porphureos describes not bright purple but the heaving, darkening surface of the sea (LSJ: 'heaving, surging'), and in phrases like 'purple death' suggests turbulence and doom. The contrast with Genesis 9:13, where the bow in the cloud is God's covenant of peace, is instructive. Leaf suspected that 17.545-6 (Zeus' 'change of mind') were added later, as Zenodotus and probably Aristarchus thought.

title: Menelaus given 'the daring of the fly'
greek: μυίης θάρσος ἐνὶ στήθεσσιν ἐνῆκεν (muiēs tharsos eni stēthessin enēken)
short: Athena, disguised as Phoenix, fills Menelaus with the boldness of a fly that keeps returning to bite however often it is brushed away.
body: Menelaus prays to Athena (not knowing she stands before him as old Phoenix), and the goddess, pleased to be invoked first, gives him strength and 'the daring of the fly': driven from a man's skin again and again, it still persists, because human blood is sweet to it. The comparison is deliberately unheroic and exact. Menelaus is not the strongest Achaean but the most dogged, and the fly's persistence matches his repeated returns to Patroclus' body. Leaf lists the Iliad's other fly similes: swarms around milk-pails (2.469-71), Athena brushing an arrow aside as a mother brushes a fly from her sleeping child (4.130-1), and men swarming round Sarpedon's corpse like flies round a milk-pail (16.641-3). Flies hover around death in the poem; Achilles later fears that flies will breed in Patroclus' wounds (19.23-7).

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, 2nd ed., vol. 2 (Macmillan, 1902), note on 17.570

title: Zeus shakes the aegis on Ida
greek: Κρονίδης ἕλετ᾽ αἰγίδα θυσσανόεσσαν ... τὴν δὲ τίναξε (Kronidēs helet' aigida thussanoessan ... tēn de tinaxe)
short: Zeus wraps Mount Ida in cloud, thunders and shakes his tasselled aegis, turning the battle in Troy's favour.
body: The turning-point of the book: Zeus takes up the aegis, the tasselled divine shield or goatskin whose shaking spreads panic (compare Apollo shaking it in 15.229-30, 15.318-22), hides Ida in cloud, lightens and thunders, and gives victory to the Trojans. The rout of the Achaeans follows at once. Leaf points to earlier descriptions of the aegis (2.447-9, 5.738-42). He also records a textual variant: Zenodotus read 'and he shook the earth' (gēn) instead of 'shook it' (tēn), whereas Leaf calls the manuscript reading very weak; Murray, like most editors, keeps the manuscript reading, 'shook the aegis'. The scene fulfils Zeus' promise to give Hector glory until sunset (17.453-5) and makes the Achaean leaders recognise that 'father Zeus himself is succouring the Trojans' (17.629-33).

title: Ajax's prayer for light
greek: ἐν δὲ φάει καὶ ὄλεσσον, ἐπεί νύ τοι εὔαδεν οὕτως (en de phaei kai olesson, epei nu toi euaden houtōs)
short: 'Father Zeus, make clear sky, and slay us in the light, since that is your pleasure': Ajax asks not for life but for light to die in.
body: Lost in the mist and unable to find a messenger for Achilles, Ajax prays: 'Father Zeus, deliver the Achaeans from the darkness, make clear sky and let us see; in the light do thou even slay us.' Zeus pities his tears and scatters the mist. Ancient critics treated the prayer as a model of greatness of soul. Pseudo-Longinus (On the Sublime 9.10) quotes it and observes that Ajax does not pray for his life, which would be beneath a hero, but for light in which to die worthily; Gregory Nagy discusses the passage and its reception. Leaf's Companion calls it 'one of the famous lines of Homer',. Leaf also wondered whether this darkness was only the dust of battle, unlike the supernatural mist of 17.268-73.

title: Antilochus, the messenger of Patroclus' death
greek: δὴν δέ μιν ἀμφασίη ἐπέων λάβε (dēn de min amphasiē epeōn labe)
short: Nestor's son, a fast runner and Achilles' friend, is struck speechless by the news and runs weeping to Achilles.
body: Menelaus chooses Antilochus, son of Nestor, to carry the news; Leaf notes he is both a close friend of Achilles and a good runner. Antilochus is stunned: 'long time was he speechless' (amphasiē), his eyes fill with tears, and he hands his armour to a comrade before running to the ships. His role has drawn attention since antiquity because of the epic tradition beyond the Iliad. In the cyclic Aethiopis Antilochus is killed by Memnon and avenged by Achilles, and the Odyssey says that Achilles honoured him most after Patroclus and that their bones lie near each other (Od. 24.76-9). Neoanalyst scholars (J. Th. Kakridis, W. Schadewaldt) argued that the Iliad's story of Patroclus, Hector and Achilles was modelled on that older Antilochus-Memnon-Achilles story; Malcolm Davies has recently re-examined and questioned such claims. Either way, the dear friend as messenger of the dearest friend's death is pointed.

title: The two Aiantes, 'one in heart as one in name'
greek: ἶσον θυμὸν ἔχοντες ὁμώνυμοι (ison thumon echontes homōnumoi)
short: Ajax son of Telamon and Ajax son of Oileus fight as a pair; the plural 'Aiantes' and the older dual 'Aiante' have long puzzled scholars.
body: The Iliad often refers to 'the Aiantes' as a unit, and here Telamonian Ajax describes himself and his namesake, the lightly armed Ajax son of Oileus (2.527-30), as 'one in heart as we are one in name' (homōnumoi), long used to standing side by side. Leaf notes that the Aiantes are always represented fighting together (note on 4.273; compare 13.701-8). The pair has a linguistic history. The dual form Aiante, as Jacob Wackernagel recognised and D. L. Page developed, could originally mean 'Ajax and his brother', that is Ajax and Teucer, by an 'elliptical' use of the dual; in our Iliad the form usually denotes the two Ajaxes, but traces of the older sense may survive (Gregory Nagy discusses the evidence). In this rearguard scene, the two Ajaxes hold back the Trojans 'as a ridge holdeth back a flood' while Menelaus and Meriones carry the body.

title: The closing cascade of similes
greek: ὥς θ᾽ ἡμίονοι κρατερὸν μένος ἀμφιβαλόντες (hōs th' hēmionoi krateron menos amphibalontes)
short: The book ends with four quick similes, fire, mules, a ridge holding back floods, and birds fleeing a falcon, for the retreat with Patroclus' body.
body: The rescue of the body is told almost entirely through a rapid sequence of similes, each catching a different aspect of the scene. The fighting rages like a fire that suddenly falls on a city, so that houses collapse in the glare (737-9), an image that anticipates the fate of Troy. Menelaus and Meriones carry the corpse like mules dragging a beam or ship's timber down a rugged mountain path, straining and sweating (742-6); Leaf explains that amphibalontes means they 'put their strength into' the load on both sides. The two Ajaxes hold back the Trojans as a wooded ridge holds back flooding rivers (747-51). The fleeing Achaean youths are like starlings or jackdaws shrieking at the sight of a falcon (755-7). The accumulation slows the narrative at the moment of greatest danger, leaving the body unresolved as the scene turns to Achilles.
